newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thais pressuring Karen rebels to hold peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Thais pressuring Karen rebels to hold peace talks.

text.p: Guerrillas of the rebel Karen National Union (KNU) said on Thursday they were under pressure from the Thai army to hold peace talks with Burma's military government.

The Thai army had pressured the KNU to shut its liaison and other offices at the Thai-Burma border and was hunting for the commander of the group's Fourth Brigade to force him to meet the Burmese government, they told Reuters.
The KNU, formed in 1948 to seek greater autonomy for the eastern Burmese Karen state, has waged a guerrilla war against Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC).

Thai authorities had turned a blind eye to the KNU's activities on the Thai side of the border in the past, but they changed their attitude towards the rebel group after Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh came to power four months ago.
Thailand has said it wants order at Karen refugee camps, which house over 90,000 refugees along its western border with Burma.
"The Thai army officers came to us and said that since we are not in a position to fight the SLORC, we should surrender," a KNU officer said in a telephone interview.
Another KNU source said the Thai army had persuaded landlords to stop having members of the rebel group as tenants.
"We have to move out by the end of this month because the landlord said the army does not allow us to live here any more," said another KNU laison officer.

Thai officers are searching for Colonel Oliver, the KNU's Fourth Brigade commander based in Burmese jungles oppposite Thailand's western Kanchanaburi province, in order to force him to make a peace agreement with Rangoon separately from the mainstream KNU.
"The Thai army said the KNU from other areas have ceased their military operations and so commander Oliver should also stop fighting," said a Karen source.
A Thai army officer, who deals with matters along the Thai-Burma border, confirmed that a search was on for Colonel Oliver to persuade him to start peace talks with Rangoon.
"Oliver is acceptable to the Burmese compared with other KNU leaders such as Bo Mya," another Thai army source said.
Bo Mya, 74, the hardline KNU commander since 1974, has been blamed by factions within his guerrilla group for recent blows to the KNU dealt by the Burmese army.
KNU sources said he had differences with his moderate and more pragmatic vice president, Swe Seing, who wanted to start negotiations with the Burmese government.
"Militarily they are separate and the personal relations between Oliver and Bo Mya are not good. So we think Oliver should make peace with Burma separately," the Thai army source said.
